query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 5 atomic percent Ti into the equal-atomic NbMoTaW refractory HEA will improve its room-temperature ductility by lowering dislocation core energies while preserving its high-temperature mechanical strength and irradiation resistance, provided that the Ti remains fully soluble in the BCC matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent high-temperature performance and predicted irradiation resistance but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition of ~5 at.% Ti.
generation.conditions: Fabricate the alloy using arc melting or selective laser melting to achieve a homogeneous NbMoTaW + 5 at.% Ti composition. Subject the material to homogenization annealing at 1600 °C to ensure complete solubility of Ti, followed by room-temperature tensile testing, high-temperature mechanical testing at approximately 1600 °C, and controlled irradiation experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and a modified dislocation core structure introduced by the substitutional Ti atoms in the BCC lattice.
generation.mechanism: Ti, which is HCP-favoring, is expected to reduce the dislocation core energy and broaden the dislocation core. This facilitates dislocation mobility at room temperature, thereby improving ductility. Simultaneously, if Ti remains fully dissolved during high-temperature annealing, the overall single-phase BCC structure is preserved, ensuring high-temperature mechanical strength and defect evolution similar to the baseline under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the alloy is anticipated to exhibit improved ductility and toughness due to enhanced dislocation glide. At 1600 °C, the high strength of the baseline NbMoTaW is expected to be maintained. Under irradiation, defect dynamics should remain comparable to the untreated alloy due to the retained BCC structure.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW refractory HEA without any Ti addition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid provided that the added ~5 at.% Ti is fully soluble in the NbMoTaW BCC matrix at 1600 °C and does not lead to the formation of secondary phases or segregation that could undermine high-temperature properties or irradiation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact phase stability and solubility of Ti in the NbMoTaW matrix at high temperatures. Experimental confirmation is required to ensure that no secondary phases form and that the irradiation resistance remains uncompromised.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sample batches of NbMoTaW with a targeted 5 at.% Ti addition using arc melting or SLM. Conduct homogenization annealing at 1600 °C to ensure full solubility and examine the phase composition using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Test the mechanical properties through room temperature tensile tests, high-temperature (1600 °C) compression/tensile tests, and subject samples to irradiation testing to compare defect evolution with the untreated baseline.
measurements: Phase analysis (XRD, TEM) to confirm single-phase BCC structure and absence of secondary phases
Room-temperature tensile ductility and toughness measurements
Irradiation-induced defect characterization (e.g., using TEM, positron annihilation spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-addition results in the formation of secondary phases or inhomogeneous microstructure after annealing at 1600 °C, or if the room-temperature ductility does not improve (or is compromised), or if irradiation tests reveal degraded defect dynamics compared to the baseline NbMoTaW, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In contrast to conventional alloys, SP-CSAs are composed of two to five-principal elements in equal or near-equal molar ratios that form random solid solutions in either a simple face-centred cubic (f.c.c.) or simple body-centred cubic (b.c.c.) crystal lattice structure. The complicated random arrangement of alloying elements and local chemical environment at atomic level lead SP-CSAs to exhibit extraordinary properties compared with traditional alloys, such as high thermal stability and hardness, high strength-to-weight ratio, high-temperature strength, great wear and fatigue resistance, and also excellent corrosion resistance. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention directly targets room‐temperature brittleness by modifying dislocation core energies, which is a root mechanism of limited ductility.
critiques.constraints: It respects the need to retain high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance provided that the Ti remains fully soluble in the BCC matrix. However, the solubility limit and phase stability at 1600 °C must be confirmed.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is plausible: minor Ti addition can induce local lattice distortions that lower dislocation core energies and enhance mobility at room temperature. The claim that Ti is HCP-favoring supports altering core structures, though verifying full solubility in the high‐temperature phase is essential.
critiques.feasibility: Using arc melting or selective laser melting with subsequent homogenization is an established method, making the approach experimentally feasible.
critiques.evidence: The supplied records (e.g., PMC5171798 and PMC6427779) support the benefits of compositional complexity in SP-CSAs for irradiation resistance and mechanical properties, but they do not directly document Ti additions in NbMoTaW.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the potential formation of secondary phases or insufficient solubility of Ti at high temperature, which could compromise the BCC single-phase stability and high-temperature properties.
critiques.fix: Perform a detailed phase stability study of NbMoTaW + ~5 at.% Ti at 1600 °C to ensure complete solubility and absence of secondary phases.

critiques.feasibility: Grain boundary engineering via controlled solidification and post-annealing is well established in materials processing, making this route feasible.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly tackles the root cause of poor room‐temperature ductility by targeting the dislocation core energy through a minor Ti addition. The mechanism—alteration of local lattice distortions by adding ~5 at.% Ti—is physically sound and is supported in principle by evidence on compositional complexity in refractory HEAs. The main risk concerns the solubility and phase stability of Ti in the BCC matrix at 1600 °C, but this can be addressed with a detailed phase stability study as a fix. Therefore, A is chosen with the proposed mitigation.
